questions.question_text: State the roots of $P(x)=(x+6)^{2}(x-3)$ and their multiplicities.

options.why: Read each root with the opposite sign — the factor $(x+6)$ is zero at $x=-6$.
Attached the square to the wrong factor; the power $2$ sits on $(x+6)$, not $(x-3)$.
Treated both factors as squared; $(x-3)$ has power $1$, so $x=3$ is a single root.

questions.solution_text:
$x=-6$, double root (the factor is squared)
$x=3$, single root

questions.question_text: Does the graph of $y=(x+2)^{3}(x-7)$ cut, bounce or inflect at $x=-2$?

options.why: A bounce needs an even power; the power here is $3$, which crosses with a flattening, not a touch.

options.text: It cuts straight through like a line
options.why: A straight cut belongs to a single root; the cubed factor flattens the curve as it crosses.
Polynomials never have asymptotes; a repeated factor changes the shape at the intercept, not the domain.

questions.solution_text:
The factor $(x+2)$ has power $3$, so $x=-2$ is a triple root.
The curve **inflects** along the axis at $x=-2$, like a cubic.

questions.question_text: Which is the monic polynomial with a double root at $x=5$ and a single root at $x=-1$?

options.why: Kept the sign of each root inside its bracket; a root at $x=5$ needs the factor $(x-5)$.
Attached the square to the wrong root; the double root is at $x=5$, not $x=-1$.
Ignored the multiplicity — a double root needs its factor squared.

questions.solution_text:
A double root at $x=5$ needs $(x-5)^{2}$; a single root at $x=-1$ needs $(x+1)$.
$P(x)=(x-5)^{2}(x+1)$

questions.question_text:
A polynomial has degree $6$ and a negative leading coefficient.
Which way do the two ends of its graph point?

options.why: Ignored the negative leading coefficient, which reflects both arms downward.

options.text: Left end up, right end down
options.why: Opposite-direction ends belong to an odd degree; degree $6$ is even, so the ends match.

options.text: Left end down, right end up
options.why: Opposite-direction ends belong to an odd degree with a positive leading term; this degree is even.

questions.solution_text:
The degree $6$ is even, so both ends point the same way.
The leading coefficient is negative, so as $x\to\pm\infty$, $y\to-\infty$: **both ends point down**.

options.why: The bounce is drawn at $2$ and the cut at $-3$ — the square sits on $(x+3)$, so the bounce belongs at $x=-3$.
This curve falls to the right, which needs a negative leading term; the leading term here is $x^{3}$.
Both roots were read with the opposite sign — this curve bounces at $3$ and cuts at $-2$.

questions.solution_text:
Roots: $x=-3$ (double, so the curve bounces) and $x=2$ (single, so the curve cuts).
Leading term $x^{3}$ rises to the right.
Sketch $A$.

questions.question_text: How does the graph of $y=P(-x)$ compare with the graph of $y=P(x)$?

options.why: That is the effect of $y=-P(x)$; replacing the input $x$ by $-x$ flips left-right, not up-down.
Replacing $x$ by $-x$ reflects the graph; a shift needs a term like $P(x-b)$ inside the function.
Only graphs symmetric in the $y$-axis are unchanged; in general each intercept $x=a$ moves to $x=-a$.

questions.solution_text: Each input $x$ is replaced by $-x$, so the graph of $y=P(-x)$ is $y=P(x)$ **reflected in the $y$-axis**.

questions.question_text: How does the graph of $y=4P(x)$ compare with the graph of $y=P(x)$?

options.text: It is stretched vertically (narrower and steeper), with the same $x$-intercepts

options.why: That is the effect of $y=P(x)+4$; multiplying by $4$ scales every $y$-value instead of adding to it.

options.text: Its $x$-intercepts move $4$ times further from the origin
options.why: The $x$-intercepts satisfy $4P(x)=0$, which happens exactly where $P(x)=0$, so they do not move.
A reflection needs a negative multiplier; $4$ is positive, so the graph keeps its direction.

questions.solution_text:
Every $y$-value is multiplied by $4$: since $|4|>1$ the graph becomes narrower (steeper).
The $x$-intercepts do not move, because $4P(x)=0$ exactly where $P(x)=0$.

questions.question_text: By factorising $y=x^{3}+8x^{2}+16x$, decide what the graph does at $x=-4$.

options.text: It cuts straight through the axis
options.why: The factorisation is $x(x+4)^{2}$ — the squared factor makes $x=-4$ a double root, which touches, not crosses.
An inflection needs a cubed factor; $(x+4)$ appears squared, so the curve bounces instead.

options.text: Nothing — the graph does not meet $x=-4$
options.why: Setting $x(x+4)^{2}=0$ gives $x=-4$ as a root, so the graph does meet the axis there.

questions.solution_text:
$y=x^{3}+8x^{2}+16x$
$=x(x^{2}+8x+16)$
$=x(x+4)^{2}$
$x=-4$ is a double root, so the curve **bounces** off the axis there.

questions.question_text:
A degree-$4$ polynomial has a triple root at $x=4$, a single root at $x=-3$, and a negative leading coefficient.
Describe its behaviour as $x\to-\infty$.

options.why: Treated the degree as odd; the multiplicities $3+1$ give degree $4$, so both ends point the same way — down.
Confused polynomial end behaviour with an asymptote; a polynomial's arms never level off.
The degree ($3+1=4$, even) and the negative leading coefficient fix both ends of the graph.

questions.solution_text:
Degree $=3+1=4$, which is even, so both ends point the same way.
The leading coefficient is negative, so both ends point down.
As $x\to-\infty$, $y\to-\infty$.
